PM’s policy is ‘Bangladesh first’, for others it is self-interest first
articles.excerpt: We fully endorse the idea of “Bangladesh First”. But don’t turn it into a mere slogan.
articles.fullText:
Now, we have a new slogan, “ Bangladesh First ”, initiated by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on behalf of the BNP in its election manifesto. In his UN speech, he added another version: “ Bangladesh for All ”. He appeared to have understood the inadequacy of the first and was wise to make it inclusive, bringing people of all ethnic and religious origins into focus. Combining the slogans—Bangladesh first and for all—can make the dream that we failed to achieve in the last 55 years of our independence worth putting all our efforts and energies behind.

What does “Bangladesh First” or “Bangladesh for All” really mean? Isn’t it about putting our national interest above our own, giving priority to things that help the nation rather than ourselves? Are we rising above self, group or partisan interests and putting the nation’s interest at the very top? Do we have the mindset to do so? Is there any precedent—except in 1971—of doing so?

The first question that people ask is whether BNP’s activities, leaders, MPs and ministers are putting Bangladesh first, before their personal and party interests. Can an MP accept a development project in a fellow MP’s area because it is needed there more? No, and their logic is that they have been elected to serve their constituencies, not those of others. It is their duty to do everything to develop the area from which they have been elected. So, can they put Bangladesh first and not their constituency?

Personal interest may be overcome, but what about party interest? Our history shows that when a party comes to power, it uses the whole state machinery to push its interests forward in every branch of the government as well as in the private sector. In fact, the argument is that party interest has become the “national interest” because “people voted for us”. This is where the conflict really gets complicated and will be very challenging for the PM to resolve.

We recently ran a story that hospital beds were being expanded in preferred districts on the basis not of public need, but of the influence of the respective leaders representing various districts . Is this putting Bangladesh first?

To turn “Bangladesh First” from a slogan into a mission, the first two things that need to be done are building institutions and fighting corruption.

What does “Bangladesh First” or “Bangladesh for All” really mean? Isn’t it about putting our national interest above our own, giving priority to things that help the nation rather than ourselves? Are we rising above self, group or partisan interests and putting the nation’s interest at the very top? Do we have the mindset to do so? Is there any precedent—except in 1971—of doing so? I mentioned in an earlier column the findings of Robinson and Acemoglu in their book Why Nations Fail . Their research, covering many countries, made it clear that only nations that build institutions can sustain their progress. If progress is individual-based, it falters as individuals do. No country can make sustainable progress if individuals come before institutions, and we stand as a good example. During the 15-plus years of Sheikh Hasina’s rule, she concentrated all powers in her hands, and others could only act to the extent the boss permitted. The police, civil service, lower judiciary and autonomous institutions were all run not only on the basis of personalities but also in line with the politics of the day.

This is in vogue again. These institutions are not being run on the principle of “Bangladesh First” but on the basis of “party and sectarian interests first”. The bureaucracy, lower judiciary, law enforcement agencies, etc are not allowed to operate as institutions whose powers and authority are clearly spelt out in government rules and procedures. Instead, they remain personality-driven, geared to serve the political power of the day and not the national interest. The functioning of all these institutions is not an example of Bangladesh first.

Take the non-governmental but meticulously legally bound institution of banks, and examine how they were run. Launched by sponsors but sustained by depositors’ money, many of them were run by the chairperson or powerful members of the board and seldom by the professional team headed by the managing director. There were clear legal distinctions between the roles of the board and management, yet, over time, they turned into private domains of the board, often in connivance with the political power of the day. This led to the bankruptcies that we are having to face now. This is what led to the huge volume of non-performing loans (NPLs)—of which Bangladesh now has the highest rate in the world —that is so crippling for our potential for growth.

The story is similar to that of public universities. Once, Dhaka University was known as the “Oxford of the East”. Today, its international ranking is better not mentioned. One of DU’s recent vice-chancellors claimed that we should be in the Guinness Book of Records because of the low price of samosa on the campus. The downturn of public universities has been largely linked to the politicisation of VC appointments. The appointees then followed the same path , only to strengthen their tenure, totally discarding merit-based recruitment, without which no university, the highest seat of learning, can have any value. Our public universities once produced the best talents for academia, bureaucracy, the judiciary, business, and other sectors. Today’s VCs are order-carriers of the education minister or ruling party leaders. After Sheikh Hasina’s fall and BNP’s return to power through the February 2026 election, most of the newly appointed VCs are known to have political leanings and thus are likely to be greatly influenced by the current ruling party and especially the leaders of its student front. Where is “Bangladesh First” here?

The other issue is corruption, which is no longer a side issue. It is threatening our future: our growth, economic strength, business sustainability, good governance, and even politics. Regrettably, we are not doing enough to fight it.

One of the established methods of stealing national resources is trade-based money laundering, which is done through over-invoicing imports and under-invoicing exports. This means that we show that we spend more on buying things from abroad and record that we earn less by selling our products in other countries. The gap between these two fictitious figures is how our precious resources are illegally sent abroad.

According to a March 2026 report by Global Financial Integrity (GFI), an international organisation monitoring illicit financial flows, around $68 billion was illegally sent out of Bangladesh between 2013 and 2022, averaging $6.8 billion a year. A 2025 study by the Bangladesh Institute of Bank Management (BIBM) found that about 75 percent of the money syphoned out of the country happened through trade-related illicit flows . The interim government’s 2024 white paper on corruption estimated that illicit outflows through all channels averaged $16 billion a year from 2009 to 2023 .

One of the established methods of stealing national resources is trade-based money laundering, which is done through over-invoicing imports and under-invoicing exports. This means that we show that we spend more on buying things from abroad and record that we earn less by selling our products in other countries. The gap between these two fictitious figures is how our precious resources are illegally sent abroad. Shouldn’t this threat be considered a national security issue by now? Here, we are literally going from door to door borrowing money to buy energy to keep our industries running, taking funds from the IMF and World Bank for budget support, and desperately trying to borrow money from anyone willing to lend to us. And here is $6.8 billion—or, according to the white paper’s estimate, $16 billion—being stolen from us annually.

What we have to understand is that the money laundering problem is not merely a financial crime. It is part of a system that operates with assured immunity and uncharacteristic efficiency compared to other administrative work. With all-round participation, it has entered every aspect of the country’s governance process. It involves our financial regulatory institutions, banking sector, high-level monitoring systems and legal framework. When these cases come under legal supervision, the process is so manipulated that what should be the most obvious step becomes mired in complex legalese and random stay orders, so that nothing really happens. And when we add to all this the subtle and not-so-subtle political patronage, it becomes clear what an integral part of our business process money laundering has become.

What strikes me as I write is that we have taken very few effective measures to stop it. Why? Maybe because it benefits all who are in power, either in terms of wealth or political clout. Today, international trade is mostly digitised. The prices of products are publicly available and can easily be confirmed. So how can our importers over-invoice anything and our exporters do the opposite? This is because we—meaning our administration, bank officials, tax collectors and political beneficiaries—help them do so. For them, Bangladesh does not come first. From the government side, what we expect is not only investigations but also public exposure and convictions. We have seen many attempts to punish these culprits, but they all end in half-hearted measures.

Here, I feel compelled to bring up the example of Nigeria. It is one of the richest—definitely in terms of natural resources, especially oil—countries in Africa. It has been so for decades, and yet Nigerians are among the poorest and its elites among the richest in the world. Why? There is a nexus between the national elites and international traders who enrich the former through Swiss bank accounts or elsewhere, while the latter are given special concessions, keeping ordinary Nigerians poor. This example is only to illustrate the nexus and nothing beyond.

If we are serious about “Bangladesh First”, then this is where we can start: putting institutions above individuals and fighting corruption.

But we know that the government cannot be solely held responsible for putting Bangladesh first. We, as individuals and professionals, must do the same. We must obey the law, not only when it suits us. We must be honest. As professionals, we must serve our clients satisfactorily. And lastly, we must pay our due taxes.

We fully endorse the idea of “Bangladesh First”. But don’t turn it into a mere slogan.

Mahfuz Anam is the editor and publisher of The Daily Star.

articles.title: US tariff threats are unfair, irrational
articles.excerpt: Bangladesh must refute the grounds for such action.
articles.fullText:
In the press release , the US, which built its economy on manufacturing in the late 1800s, accused Bangladesh of being unreasonable in its policy to expand its industrial base through manufacturing and exports. Besides, the allegation that Bangladesh’s policies in the apparel sector are reducing US commercial opportunities is also preposterous, as Bangladesh is not even a direct competitor of the US. Moreover, the accusation of excess capacity and production has already been refuted by BGMEA in April, when the allegation first surfaced. Besides, accusing an economy of leveraging its competitive advantage by sourcing inputs from countries offering more competitive prices in the international market is simply hypocritical of the US, which champions free market principles.

And to think, the newly proposed tariffs don’t even seem to consider the fact that Bangladesh already signed a reciprocal trade agreement with the US earlier in February in good faith, conceding to problematic terms and conditions in several areas. The latest announcement is thus nothing short of an attempt by a superpower to hold a developing country hostage through economic coercion.

The timing of the announcement could not have been worse. Bangladesh is already reeling under persistent inflation, made worse by high energy costs—a crisis for which the US is largely responsible and poorer, energy-dependent nations are paying the price. Production costs are already high for domestic industries, with higher interest rates and energy prices. Nor have they been able to secure better prices from buyers, which have arguably declined over the years. Besides, the ongoing labour unrest in the RMG sector is taking a toll on production and export orders.

A higher tariff rate, if implemented, would undoubtedly increase costs for US importers, resulting in decreased RMG orders. This could happen even though many of our competitors in the apparel sector are facing similar tariffs and may not be able to beat our competitive prices. Under such scenarios, how could Bangladeshi exporters pay better wages and improve the very labour conditions that the US preaches?

Therefore, it is imperative that the government present an evidence-based response to USTR’s allegations. At the same time, Bangladesh must urgently work towards market and product diversification so that no single trade partner is influential enough to compel us to cater to their economic interests instead of our own.

articles.title: What Bangladesh can learn from Japan’s waste management system
articles.excerpt: In Bangladesh, we frequently discuss public awareness, but how often do we systematically teach residents how to manage household waste?
articles.fullText:
One of the first things I have noticed in Japan is the absence of public dustbins. In Hong Kong, public bins are relatively easy to find and municipal workers regularly empty them. In Dhaka or Khulna, however, dustbins are often insufficient, poorly maintained, or surrounded by accumulated rubbish. Japan manages to keep its streets and surroundings remarkably clean despite having relatively few dustbins. The reason is not merely efficient municipal services, but also a system that places responsibility on individuals for managing their waste properly.

I was particularly impressed by how seriously waste management is introduced to newcomers in Fukuoka. When international students arrive at Kyushu University, waste disposal rules are an important part of their introduction. Dormitory managers explain how rubbish should be separated, which bags to use, and where waste can be discarded. The university's orientation activities also help students understand these local regulations.

This may appear to be a minor administrative matter, but it reflects an important principle: people cannot be expected to follow rules they have never been taught properly. In Bangladesh, we frequently discuss public awareness, but how often do we systematically teach residents how to manage household waste? We may organise occasional cleaning campaigns, but the everyday practices responsible for generating rubbish receive far less attention. Consider how household waste is commonly collected at residential buildings in Bangladeshi cities. Residents leave their rubbish outside their doors, usually in plastic bags. A caretaker collects these bags from different floors and brings them downstairs. Often, the waste is temporarily piled near the building's entrance until a rickshaw-van collector or another collection service arrives. Although this arrangement removes waste from individual residences, it creates another problem at the main gate. Kitchen scraps, plastic packaging, broken glass, and other discarded materials are frequently mixed. Bags may tear, resulting in leaks and unpleasant smells.

Importantly, the rules are properly enforced. Bags that don’t meet the city's requirements may be left uncollected with a warning sticker. The collection point may differ between residential buildings and neighbourhoods, but the underlying responsibility remains clear: waste must be managed properly before it is handed over to the collection system.

During my visit to Sustaina Kyoto, what struck me most was an environmental education facility connected to Kyoto's Southern Clean Center. The facility demonstrates how modern waste treatment can support resource recovery and energy generation. Its infrastructure includes waste incineration, resource sorting, and biogas production. Heat from incineration is used to generate electricity, while biodegradable materials processed through anaerobic digestion can produce biogas for power generation.

Witnessing these processes first-hand helped me realise that waste management is not necessarily just an expenditure for local authorities. With appropriate technology and planning, waste can also contribute to energy production and resource recovery. However, such facilities require considerable investment, technical expertise, and reliable operational systems. Bangladesh may not simply replicate Japan's infrastructure overnight. What we can learn immediately is the importance of separating waste before it reaches a processing facility.

Bangladesh already has an advantage that deserves greater attention: its established network of household caretakers, community waste collectors, and rickshaw-vans. Rather than replacing this system, city corporations could improve it. A practical start could be a two-bin or two-bag system: one for organic kitchen waste and the other for dry recyclable materials. Hazardous household items and broken glass would require separate and safe disposal arrangements. Residents would separate waste inside their homes. Caretakers would collect it without mixing the categories, and designated collection vehicles would transport the materials separately.

Such changes would require public education, affordable collection materials, regular supervision, and clear responsibilities for households, building managers, and waste collectors. Municipalities would also need to ensure that separately collected waste is not mixed again during transportation. The approach could initially be tested in selected neighbourhoods before being expanded. Organic waste could be directed towards composting or suitable biogas facilities, while recyclable materials could enter established recycling channels. Most importantly, properly contained and regularly collected waste would reduce the unhygienic piles that often accumulate around residential buildings or in public spaces.

The experience in Fukuoka has convinced me that clean cities are not created through infrastructure alone. They also require clear rules, consistent implementation, and cooperation between residents and local authorities. We need to examine our existing practices and make realistic changes suited to our own circumstances. Perhaps the most important lesson is that the journey to a cleaner city may begin with the simple decision not to mix everything in the same bag.

Md Ayatullah Khan is a doctoral researcher in the Department of Geography at Hong Kong Baptist University in Hong Kong, and an exchange PhD student and visiting researcher at Kyushu University in Japan.

articles.title: Healthcare should not come at the cost of financial security
articles.excerpt: The burden is particularly severe for disadvantaged communities. In 2022, around 90.8 percent of people in the poorest 20 percent of the population faced financial hardship due to healthcare spending.
articles.fullText:
For many, the financial burden of illness becomes almost as distressing as the illness itself. More than 1.08 crore Bangladeshis , representing 6.4 percent of the population, fell below the poverty line in 2022 because of out-of-pocket (OOP) healthcare expenses—almost double the number in 2005. This increase is particularly concerning because the national poverty rate declined from 40 percent to 18.7 percent during the same period. The proportion of people facing financial hardship due to healthcare spending increased from 28.2 percent in 2005 to 41.7 percent in 2022.

The findings come from a study by the Health Economics Unit (HEU) under the health ministry, conducted with support from World Health Organization (WHO) and the Swedish Embassy. The study analysed four rounds of Household Income and Expenditure Survey data from 2005, 2010, 2016-17 and 2022, and revealed that average monthly household OOP healthcare expenditure, adjusted for inflation, increased from Tk 1,241 in 2005 to Tk 3,238 in 2022. The proportion of households reporting healthcare expenditure from their own pockets also rose from 52.5 percent to 92.7 percent. Meanwhile, catastrophic health expenditure increased from 12.5 percent to 32.1 percent.

The burden is particularly severe for disadvantaged communities. In 2022, around 90.8 percent of people in the poorest 20 percent of the population faced financial hardship due to healthcare spending, compared with just 13.6 percent among the richest 20 percent. The rate was 47.9 percent in rural areas, against 28.2 percent in urban areas, with Barishal Division recording the highest rate at 59.1 percent.

Another worrying trend is the growing dependence on pharmacies for outpatient care. Their share of outpatient healthcare provision increased from 32.5 percent in 2016 to 55.4 percent in 2022. Pharmacies play an important role in healthcare delivery, but this trend raises questions about access to qualified medical advice, proper diagnosis, and safe medicine use. Gaps in primary healthcare can increase the risks of unnecessary medication, antibiotic misuse, and delayed diagnosis, ultimately adding to household and national healthcare costs.

Public hospitals remain the main providers of inpatient care, but their share declined from 61.3 percent in 2016 to 56 percent in 2022. Meanwhile, the private sector's share increased from 36.9 percent to 42.5 percent. The study also raises concerns that publicly funded healthcare benefits are not adequately reaching poorer households. If public resources disproportionately benefit relatively better-off groups, increased healthcare spending alone will not reduce inequality.

What needs to change, then? First, the government must increase public healthcare financing and ensure its effective use. Budget allocations should prioritise preventive healthcare, primary care, essential medicines, and diagnostic services. Upazila health complexes and union-level health facilities need adequate health workers, essential medicines, reliable diagnostic facilities, and effective referral systems.

Second, Bangladesh needs a functional financial protection mechanism for vulnerable households. National health insurance or social health protection programmes should be expanded gradually, prioritising poor families, older people, persons with disabilities, people living with chronic illnesses, and workers in the informal sector. The government could fully subsidise premiums for poor households. Financing arrangements, benefit packages, service quality, and accountability mechanisms must be clearly defined before implementation.

Third, access to essential medicines and diagnostic tests must become more affordable. Free medicine policies must translate into actual availability at public hospitals. Transparent procurement, effective supply chains, and proper stock management are essential. Public hospital laboratories also need modernisation, quality control, and timely test results to reduce patients' dependence on expensive private diagnostic facilities.

Fourth, healthcare governance must become more accountable and evidence-driven. The HEU, Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics, and Directorate General of Health Services should establish a coordinated national monitoring system. Regular data should show how many families fall into poverty because of medical expenses, which regions face the greatest financial hardship, which illnesses incur the highest costs, and who benefits from public healthcare spending.

Ultimately, healthcare must not be treated as a luxury; it is a fundamental human right. No one should have to choose between receiving medical treatment and protecting their family's future savings. The state's responsibility goes beyond building hospitals and appointing doctors. It must ensure that every citizen can access quality healthcare without falling into poverty.

Ensure healthcare reaches the poorest
articles.excerpt: Address the growing inequality in access to public health services
articles.fullText:
According to the Health Economics Unit (HEU) under the health ministry, in 2016, the poorest two of five wealth groups received 46 percent of inpatient services benefits at public hospitals, compared with 28 percent for the richest two groups. By 2022, the situation had reversed, with the poorest groups receiving only 33 percent of the benefits while the richest received 38 percent. A similar disparity was reported in outpatient services, with the richest two groups consistently receiving a greater share of benefits than the poorest two. The question is: what is making middle- and upper-income groups depend more on public hospitals?

The answer lies partly in rising out-of-pocket (OOP) healthcare expenditure—the money households pay directly for healthcare, including medicines, diagnostic tests, and treatment. Reportedly, OOP expenditure pushed over 1.08 crore people below the poverty line in 2022, almost double the 56 lakh recorded in 2005, despite the national poverty rate declining from 40 percent to 18.7 percent. Financial hardship due to healthcare spending also increased from 28.2 percent in 2005 to 41.7 percent in 2022, significantly exceeding the global estimate of 26 percent.

Under these circumstances, while low-income households are forced to take loans, sell assets or even compromise on treatment, relatively better-off people are also increasingly relying on public hospitals. People’s dependence on pharmacies for treatment has also increased, suggesting that many are seeking alternatives to formal healthcare facilities. Meanwhile, political and social connections can also influence access to public services, allowing influential groups to enjoy advantages meant for the poorest people.

The government must urgently address this growing inequality if public healthcare is to serve its intended purpose. It must strengthen primary healthcare, ensure transparent and needs-based allocation of public health resources, and take effective measures to improve healthcare access for the poorest. More public investment is also needed to reduce households’ out-of-pocket expenditure and make essential treatment affordable for all.

articles.title: Getting our industrial policy right before LDC graduation
articles.excerpt: The UN General Assembly’s decision to give Bangladesh an extension through November 2029 before it formally graduates from the group of least developed countries (LDCs) is a window of opportunity for Bangladesh to recalibrate its industrial policy to build a competitive, diversified and job-friendly economy.
articles.fullText:
The first proposition is what I call the Goldilocks balance: combining broad public inputs that benefit all sectors and firms with a small number of deliberate bets on future winners. The first stream of this Goldilocks balance is to tackle structural constraints that are holding back private sector growth: a financial sector that provides affordable working capital and long-term finance, reliable energy, market-driven skills, and predictable investment rules. These should be complemented by addressing procedural bottlenecks, including faster customs clearance, clearer product standards, credible testing and certification, and simpler licensing. These fixes can create a level playing field that rewards exporting and benefits new entrants and small firms, not just established businesses.

The second stream is a limited portfolio of deliberate bets supporting sub-sectors selected against clear criteria such as high growth potential, job creation and backward linkages to small enterprises. Here the Goldilocks logic applies again: enough support for infant or emerging industries to learn, but not so much that firms come to depend on subsidies and high tariffs for survival. Successful industrial policy in Asia may have given the impression of heavy protection and boundless state benevolence, but in many cases, support came with strings , including export targets, domestic competition and expectations of technological upgrading and learning spillovers to smaller enterprises. Bangladesh’s own experience of industrial policy weakly tied to performance shows that state support can become entrenched, benefiting incumbents and creating barriers to entry for new businesses. Transparent, time-bound support with sunset clauses can, therefore, act as a counterweight to these political economy constraints.

The second proposition is that industrial policy must look beyond manufacturing. Bangladesh’s next stage of development should rest on a Goldilocks balance of economic sectors: productive agriculture, competitive manufacturing and modern services. The unifying objective is productivity, not necessarily a preferred sector. Manufacturing’s capacity for job creation and rapid productivity gains has traditionally made it the core of industrial policy, and it remains crucial for structural transformation. But its share of the global economy has been shrinking in nominal terms, and in many economies, services now account for the largest share of GDP and jobs. The catch, however, is that productivity gains in services are harder to achieve and often confined to a few high-value activities. In Bangladesh, services, many of them low-value, generate over half of GDP , while agriculture still employs the largest share of workers, around 45 percent . But the boundaries between sectors are also blurring. Digital technologies are integrating manufacturing more closely with services: factories depend on software, finance, design, logistics, testing, maintenance and marketing. Similarly, agricultural upgrading creates demand for processing, storage and distribution. The task, therefore, is not a hard choice between sectors but raising productivity across all of them, while deepening capabilities in those that Bangladesh has identified as strategic , such as pharmaceuticals, agro-processing and light engineering.

The third proposition is that none of this works without the state capability to deliver it, and this is where Bangladesh faces its steepest climb. Industrial policy demands a different kind of statecraft: not only design but also highly effective execution, monitoring of results, experimentation under uncertainty and course correction when needed. While state capability is difficult to define or measure, some illustrations show the implementation deficits that Bangladesh faces. For example, implementation of the Annual Development Programme (ADP) remains weak. In FY2025-26, only 67.5 percent of the revised ADP budget was utilised, the lowest rate in 53 years . At a provisional 6.8 percent in FY2025-26, Bangladesh’s tax-to-GDP ratio is abnormally low even by developing-country standards. Direct tax exemptions alone cost 2.4 percent of GDP in FY2022-23, almost as much as the state collected in personal and corporate income taxes that year. Economists Khondker and Nandi (2025) have also argued that the benefits of these exemptions are diffuse, poorly targeted and weakly monitored. All this points to suboptimal tax policy and weak administration.

Building state capability for policy execution tends to get the least attention. Successful industrialisers invested in capabilities and governance as they progressed. An important point here is to avoid falling into the trap of what international development scholars Pritchett, Woolcock and Andrews (2013) call isomorphic mimicry: creating institutions that take the form but cannot perform the function well. A practical lesson is to build a few “islands of excellence” within a ministry or as an inter-ministerial unit as a short-term fix to offset capacity deficits while investing in wider systems and institutional improvements. Investments in capacity development can take different forms, ranging from restructuring organisations and workflows to training of personnel to financial resources. Moreover, effective functioning of institutions requires transparency and accountability tied to performance metrics that are applied consistently and monitored.

The three-year extension does not change LDC graduation as the destination. It only gives Bangladesh more time to prepare for what the Smooth Transition Strategy calls a “high road” to future growth: an economic transformation that relies less on low costs and trade preferences than on competitiveness, productivity and decent jobs. Getting to the destination means broad public goods that lift all firms, a few disciplined bets with strings attached, a productivity lens from farms and factories to services, and the state’s capability to deliver what it designs.

Owais Parray is country economic adviser at United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), Bangladesh.

articles.title: The failure of climate leadership is a failure of gender justice, too
articles.excerpt: After almost 50 hours of overtime, COP31 in Antalya closed without agreement on its overarching political outcome. Negotiations failed because of a lack of political courage to act. What stayed with me was the “poverty of leadership”.
articles.fullText:
UN Secretary-General António Guterres expected governments to rise to the demands of the climate crisis. But the proposed Antalya Pact could not bridge the divide over fossil fuels, climate finance, and the response to the 1.5 degrees Celsius overshoot. The science was clear and the consequences were visible, yet governments could not agree on the scale of action required.

COP31 should be judged by its impact on the people whose lives remain exposed when governments leave the conference. For communities on the climate frontline, homes disappear, livelihoods are lost, and women absorb the shock through unpaid care, longer working days, depleted savings, and the work of keeping families alive.

To be clear, COP31 adopted decisions on adaptation, the Adaptation Fund, and the Just Transition Work Programme. However, the failure to agree on the Antalya Pact and the rejection of other proposed decisions revealed how difficult it has become to pursue ambitious climate action amid competing fossil fuel interests, narrow national priorities, and finance disputes. A process built on consensus can easily become a means of obstructing progress. Multilateralism is indispensable, but it must not become an excuse for inaction.

The feminist failure is not confined to the absence of gender language. It is embedded in the political economy of climate response. When public systems fail, women fill the gaps: securing water, caring for the sick, finding food, rebuilding homes, and holding communities together. Their unpaid labour effectively compensates for the failure of governments and economies to bear the true cost of climate damage. This is not freely chosen resilience, but rather a transfer of public responsibility onto women.

Women are routinely described as vulnerable, while the structures producing that vulnerability escape scrutiny. They are invited to share experiences, but too often excluded from decisions about money, land, energy, and recovery. The Belém Gender Action Plan remains in place, but implementation cannot rest on aspiration. Without adequate funding, protection for women environmental defenders, and accountability for implementation, the plan risks celebrating women’s agency without addressing existing power imbalances. It is the politics of asking women to endure more.

The same contradiction runs through climate finance. Countries failed to agree on a clear baseline, a quantified pathway, or a delivery plan for the commitment to at least triple adaptation finance by 2035. The proposed $120 billion annual figure did not make it in the final negotiating text. For Bangladesh, this means continued uncertainty for adaptation to floods, cyclones, salinity, and extreme heat, as well as continued pressure on public budgets, local institutions, and households already financing their own survival.

Moreover, parties extended the Just Transition Work Programme (JTWP) but postponed decisions on the functions and operational arrangements of the proposed mechanism until COP32. Workers, women in informal employment, small producers, and communities dependent on fossil-fuel economies need more than dialogue: decent work, social protection, affordable clean energy, skills, public investment, and a decisive voice in shaping change. A transition that leaves these guarantees unfunded is not just.

So, what needs to happen before COP32 in Addis Ababa? First, developed countries must put forward a time-bound plan for public, grant-based climate finance, with clear baselines, milestones, and accountability. Adaptation and loss and damage cannot be financed by pushing vulnerable countries further into debt.

Second, governments must turn the just transition commitment into an operational mechanism with predictable finance and worker- and community-centred safeguards. The transition away from fossil fuels must be real, planned, and equitable, not delayed by false solutions or promises of future technology.

Third, gender commitments must be financed and measured. Women’s organisations, Indigenous peoples, young people, and frontline communities need direct access to resources and decision-making. Women environmental defenders must be protected, because participation cannot happen without participation.

Finally, governments must confront the influence of fossil fuel interests and stop using consensus to dilute urgency. Those most responsible for emissions must lead in cutting them and financing the response. Those least responsible must not be made to pay twice: first by suffering climate destruction, and then through debt.

For Bangladesh, the road to Addis Ababa must also mean defending fiscal space, securing climate reparations, and investing in locally led adaptation, not borrowing to survive a crisis it did not create. The choice is not between defending multilateralism and criticising its failures. We need a stronger multilateral process capable of delivering precisely because climate change crosses borders.

Antalya should be remembered as the moment governments were asked to choose between protecting an exhausted political bargain and protecting people. They failed that test. The road to Addis Ababa must be measured in finance delivered, fossil fuels left behind, rights protected, and power redistributed. Anything less is another year in which governments negotiate while women do the work of survival.

Farah Kabir is country director at ActionAid Bangladesh

articles.title: Amid a rebound in megaprojects, the govt must rethink spending and foreign borrowing
articles.excerpt: The BNP-led government has embarked on a series of costly megaprojects, although it said it wouldn’t.
articles.fullText:
But since taking office, the BNP-led government has embarked on a series of costly megaprojects. These include the Tk 34,497.25 crore Padma Barrage ; one new metro rail project and revisions to two others in Dhaka costing Tk 2,50,000 crore ; a new Dhaka-Cumilla elevated railway costing Tk 84,000 crore ; and the Dhaka-Chattogram Expressway costing Tk 1,25,000 crore . The government has also decided in principle to build a second Padma Bridge and a second Jamuna Bridge.

The previous Awami League government also undertook numerous foreign debt-funded megaprojects that failed to deliver their expected benefits, generate projected revenues or create sufficient employment, while substantially increasing the country’s external debt burden. The new projects raise similar economic, technical and environmental concerns, including questions about their economic viability and timing. These are being pursued when government expenditure and foreign debt are rising faster than revenue.

Government spending has surged after public servants’ salaries rose by 100-142 percent. Once the new pay structure is fully implemented, annual salary and allowance expenditure will rise by an additional Tk 1,05,000 crore from January 2028. The government is also planning three costly LNG terminals, which will further increase foreign currency expenditure on LNG imports.

Revenue shortfalls and mounting debt repayment pressures

Meanwhile, revenue collection is failing to keep pace. In the first three months of FY2026-27, the National Board of Revenue (NBR) fell Tk 41,879 crore short of its target. Against a target of Tk 1,34,396 crore, it collected only Tk 92,517 crore—about 31 percent below the target.

Bangladesh’s tax-to-GDP ratio is already exceptionally low. According to IMF , it stood at 8.34 percent in 2024, compared with 20 percent in India, 13 percent in Pakistan, 14 percent in Sri Lanka and 27 percent in Bhutan. Rising expenditure amid weak revenue growth has driven up both domestic and external debt, increasing debt-servicing costs that are expected to rise further. According to Bangladesh Bank, government domestic debt reached Tk 11,53,635 crore at the end of FY2025-26, an increase of approximately Tk 1,32,000 crore in a single year.

External debt has also reached an unprecedented level. The World Bank’s International Debt Report 2026 puts Bangladesh’s total external debt stock, including both public and private debt, at $113.43 billion at the end of 2025—equivalent to approximately Tk 14 lakh crore at current exchange rates. In 2015, it stood at $38.77 billion. Bangladesh’s external debt has therefore nearly tripled in a decade.

Debt servicing is becoming an increasingly heavy burden. Bangladesh repaid $4.5 billion in external debt in FY2025-26 and another $1.35 billion in the first three months of the current fiscal year, from July to September. Annual repayments could exceed $5 billion this year and $7 billion by 2030 , putting substantial pressure on foreign exchange reserves.

But the government’s plans show little sign of caution. Instead of abandoning expensive, foreign debt-funded megaprojects of lower priority, it is pursuing new ones while borrowing abroad to finance routine budget deficits. For example, the government is borrowing $1 billion from the World Bank to purchase fertiliser and fuel. It has also sought $1 billion in budget support from the Asian Development Bank (ADB) and $4.5 billion from the IMF.

More concerningly, alongside concessional loans from bilateral and multilateral lenders, the government is considering raising foreign currency through sovereign bonds in international capital markets. Such commercial borrowing at high interest rates would expose the economy to greater risks.

Dollar-denominated sovereign bonds typically have maturities of only five to 10 years and interest rates exceeding 6 percent. Interest is paid twice a year, but the principal must be repaid in full at maturity, creating a substantial foreign exchange obligation. Reliance on these bonds also exposes the country to assessments by international credit rating agencies, whose evaluations can be opaque and influenced by geopolitical considerations.

By contrast, although concessional loans from governments and multilateral institutions such as the World Bank come with conditions, they generally carry interest rates of 0.25-3 percent, maturities of 20-40 years and grace periods. Principal and interest can be repaid in instalments over many years, easing pressure on foreign exchange reserves.

The greatest strain arises when sovereign bonds mature, as the entire principal must be repaid in foreign currency at once, putting the balance of payments under severe pressure. With fewer restrictions on how bond proceeds are spent, governments may also use them for consumer imports or wasteful projects.

The danger is borrowing in foreign currency for five or 10 years to finance activities that generate insufficient foreign exchange to repay the principal and interest. Long-term projects may also take years to generate returns, while the bonds mature much earlier. This is known as a maturity mismatch . Such borrowing can quickly become an unsustainable burden, prompting governments to issue new sovereign bonds to repay old ones and accumulate ever more debt. Sri Lanka’s experience illustrates this danger.

In 2007, Sri Lanka issued its first international sovereign bond (ISB), raising $500 million at an interest rate of 8.25 percent for five years. It subsequently increased its borrowing, with a substantial portion of new bond proceeds used to service earlier bonds. Between 2011 and 2019, it issued sovereign bonds 13 times , ranging from $500 million to $1.5 billion, with maturities ranging from five to 11 years. ISBs accounted for just 4.3 percent of Sri Lanka’s external debt in 2007. By the end of 2019, their share had risen to 48.2 percent .

The country eventually faced a situation in which it lacked sufficient foreign exchange to import essentials such as food and fuel, yet had to deplete its reserves to meet sovereign debt obligations. In January 2022 , for example, Sri Lanka had to repay a $500 million bond issued in 2012, despite being in the midst of a severe economic crisis.

Its foreign exchange reserves stood at around $2 billion in 2022, while total external debt repayments due that year amounted to approximately $7 billion .

Sri Lanka eventually suspended external debt repayments and was forced to negotiate a debt restructuring agreement with the IMF. The resulting economic collapse inflicted severe hardship on its people. To avoid a similar crisis, Bangladesh must halt plans to raise dollar-denominated debt through sovereign bonds.

Caution is necessary not only with sovereign bonds but with all external borrowing. Foreign currency loans for projects that fail to generate sufficient foreign exchange for repayment can become a growing burden. A low debt-to-GDP ratio alone is no guarantee of safety. Since external debt must be repaid in foreign currency, the government must assess whether export earnings and foreign exchange reserves can grow sufficiently relative to external debt, and whether government revenue and export income will be adequate to cover principal and interest payments.

The government must strengthen domestic revenue mobilisation, prioritising direct taxation of those with greater ability to pay rather than placing a disproportionate burden on ordinary people through value-added tax (VAT).

It should also refrain from unnecessary, expensive, foreign debt-funded megaprojects, rigorously assess the economic returns, and potential foreign exchange earnings of any new project, and prioritise public spending on essential sectors such as education and healthcare. Without these changes, rising debt and costly borrowing could undermine Bangladesh’s economic stability and leave future generations with an increasingly heavy burden.

articles.title: Shastho Batayon helpline: Why let a lifeline to healthcare fall silent over unpaid bills?
articles.excerpt: Rahim Mia returns to his village home at about 10:30pm and finds his five-year-old daughter’s fever getting worse.
articles.fullText:
For more than a decade, a poor farmer’s wife in a char village, a day labourer in a slum, or a mother awake late at night with her feverish child could pick up a phone, dial 16263, and reach a qualified doctor—free of fees. But on November 12 this year, the line went quiet, at a time when access to affordable medical care remains out of reach for many, particularly in rural and underserved areas and when dengue and measles cases remain high. The operator, Synesis IT, stopped the service after its contract with the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) lapsed, and the health ministry has since said it intends to resume it. But how did a service which helped millions come to an end in the first place?

Few services in Bangladesh’s health system have been as simple and as useful as a free phone call to a doctor. Shastho Batayon 16263, a free national 24/7 health helpline run through the DGHS, reached nearly three crore people since it began operating in 2015. In the first phase of the Covid pandemic alone, between March and December 2020, the line received 1.26 crore calls. Even between May 2 to October 31 of this year, an average of 6,137 calls were received by the helpline each day, with around 100 MBBS doctors and 25 health information officers working in shifts. A presentation by the DGHS to the WHO shows that nearly three-quarters of the 1.6 crore services recorded between March 2020 and January 2023 contained doctors’ advice and treatment. These are not the figures of a marginal programme.

The cost of seeking healthcare in Bangladesh includes more than just the doctor’s fee. There is the bus or boat fare, lost wages, the time of the relative who must accompany a sick child or an elderly person, and the long wait at an upazila health complex or district hospital. For a family in a remote area, the nearest qualified doctor may be hours away. Too often, the alternative is the village pharmacy, an informal practitioner, or simply waiting. A phone call to the hotline offers a crucial alternative. A doctor can say what can be managed at home, what the community clinic can handle, and what needs a hospital that very night. For poor families, the greatest danger is delay, and a free call is among the cheapest ways to shorten it.

What went wrong was not a lack of demand. The health secretary has said the ministry never meant to shut the service, but that it struggled to arrange the funds to pay the operator more than Tk 16 crore in outstanding dues. Reports earlier this year said the ministry had not released money to the operator for 17 months. The sector programme that funded the service expired in June 2024, and its planned successor was scrapped in March 2025. Since then, a service that millions relied on has had no secure budget. Health sector experts warned and stated that with no alternative in place, it is the poor who will bear the cost.

The money, moreover, is not an obstacle. The FY2026-27 budget raises the health allocation to Tk 69,409 crore, nearly double last year’s revised Tk 35,477 crore and, at 1.01 percent of GDP, the first time it has crossed 1 percent. Yet in the first quarter, from July to September, the Health Services Division spent only Tk 107 crore of its Tk 6,014 crore development allocation, or 1.78 percent, against a national rate of 3.89 percent that was itself a record low. Tk 16 crore in dues is well under 1 percent of what is still to be spent.

Moreover, BNP’s election manifesto promised to bring health services to every doorstep. A phone line that reaches the poor and remote areas is the fastest way to do that. Beyond giving advice directly to patients, 16263 could serve as the hub of a hub-and-spoke referral network. The doctor on the line would advise callers, refer those who need an in-person visit to the nearest community clinic, union health centre, or upazila health complex, or, when needed, pass the case to a district or tertiary hospital. This way, callers would not have to start over at each stage.

Bangladesh is not asking for anything unusual. India’s eSanjeevani , a free national telemedicine service, has crossed 50 crore consultations, with rural patients far outnumbering urban ones. Pakistan’s Sindh government funds Tele-Tabeeb 1123 , a free round-the-clock line to doctors. Sri Lanka now fully funds its 1990 ambulance service, while Bhutan offers health advice when citizens dial 112. These countries differ in income and size, but each keeps such services on a standing government budget, not an expiring project. Bangladesh was early in the region; it would be a pity to let its lifeline go dead. Hence, restoring the line is the first step, but a temporary restart is not enough. The Shastho Batayon hotline should be placed in the national budget with a multi-year allocation, so that it never again depends on an expiring project.

A country that aspires to universal health coverage cannot let one of its cheapest and most far-reaching services for the poor and the remote disappear over unpaid bills. The dues are small against the value the service has delivered. Telemedicine, ICT-based, and AI-supported health services are the future of our health sector, and Shastho Batayon is the foundation on which they can be built. The government must restore the line, secure consistent funding, and make sure callers get the help they need. Each day of delay makes the service harder and more expensive to bring back, so the decision should not wait.

M Morshed Alam is programme manager of Bangladesh Health Watch at James P Grant School of Public Health, BRAC University.

articles.title: আফগানিস্তানে ঘরে ঘরে নারীদের ‘গোপন লড়াই’
articles.excerpt: আফগানিস্তানের রাজধানী কাবুলের ব্যস্ত সড়কের আড়ালে লুকিয়ে আছে এক গোপন জগৎ। ২০২১ সালের আগস্টে মার্কিন নেতৃত্বাধীন সেনা প্রত্যাহারের পর তালেবান ক্ষমতা দখল করলে নারীদের ওপর যে কঠোর নিষেধাজ্ঞা জারি করা হয়, নীরবে তা অমান্য করে চলেছেন সেই নারীরা।
articles.fullText: আফগানিস্তানের রাজধানী কাবুলের ব্যস্ত সড়কের আড়ালে লুকিয়ে আছে এক গোপন জগৎ। ২০২১ সালের আগস্টে মার্কিন নেতৃত্বাধীন সেনা প্রত্যাহারের পর তালেবান ক্ষমতা দখল করলে নারীদের ওপর যে কঠোর নিষেধাজ্ঞা জারি করা হয়, নীরবে তা অমান্য করে চলেছেন সেই নারীরা। ইসলামি ধর্মীয় শিক্ষা ও ভাষার কোর্স ছাড়া প্রাথমিক স্তরের পর নারীদের পড়াশোনা নিষিদ্ধ। পার্ক ও ব্যায়ামাগারে যাওয়া মানা, বিউটি সেলুন বেআইনি ঘোষণা করা হয়েছে এবং আপাদমস্তক কঠোর পোশাকবিধি চালু রয়েছে। নারীরা কিছু ব্যবসায়িক লাইসেন্স নিতে পারলেও অধিকাংশ কাজ থেকেই তাঁরা বঞ্চিত। খেলাধুলার ওপর নিষেধাজ্ঞায় স্বপ্ন ভেঙে যাওয়া সাবেক এক ফুটবলার বলেন, ‘আফগানিস্তানে নারী হওয়াটাই এক অপরাধ।’ সৎ কাজের প্রসার ও অসৎ কাজের প্রতিরোধ মন্ত্রণালয়ের নীতি-পুলিশ এসব নিয়ম কার্যকর করে। তাঁরা বেশ ভীতিকর। চিকিৎসকদের মতো সাদা গাউন পরে তাঁরা রাস্তায় টহল দেন এবং নিয়ম ভাঙলে নারীদের আটক করতে পারেন। কাউকে কাউকে মারধরও করা হয়েছে। পাকিস্তান-আফগানিস্তান সম্পর্কের অবনতি যেসব কারণে ভারত–আফগানিস্তান: ‘হিন্দুবাদী’ ও ‘ইসলামি’ দুটি দেশের সম্পর্কের রসায়ন নারীদের ওপর বিধিনিষেধ নিয়ে এপির প্রশ্নের জবাবে মন্ত্রণালয়ের মুখপাত্র মোহাম্মদ আসলাম বদ্রিওয়াল বলেন, ইসলামি শরিয়া আইনের আওতায় সবার অধিকার নিশ্চিত করতে মন্ত্রণালয় ‘পুরোপুরি অঙ্গীকারবদ্ধ’। মোহাম্মদ আসলাম বদ্রিওয়াল বলেন, ‘ইসলামি শরিয়াহর নীতিমালা এবং বর্তমানে কার্যকর আইন কঠোরভাবে মেনে চললে আমাদের বোনেরা তাঁদের সামাজিক ও বাণিজ্যিক কর্মকাণ্ডও পরিচালনা করতে পারেন।’ তিনি আরও যোগ করেন, সমাজে তাঁদের বোনদের পুরোপুরি নিরাপত্তা নিশ্চিত করা এবং শরিয়াপ্রদত্ত সব অধিকার ভোগ করার সুযোগ দেওয়াই মন্ত্রণালয়ের অগ্রাধিকার। ঝুঁকি সত্ত্বেও কিছু নারী এসব নিষেধাজ্ঞা অমান্য করার উপায় খুঁজে নিয়েছেন। কাবুলের এমনই তিন নারীর গোপন জীবনের খণ্ডচিত্র নিচে তুলে ধরা হলো। গ্রেপ্তারের ভয়ে তাঁরা সবাই নাম প্রকাশ না করার শর্তে কথা বলেছেন। চল্লিশ বছর বয়সী এক নারী বহু বছর কাবুলের একটি বিউটি সেলুনে কাজ করেছেন। তালেবান কর্তৃপক্ষ সেলুন নিষিদ্ধ করলে তাঁর মনে হয়, জীবনটা যেন সংকুচিত হয়ে গেল। গোপনে ঘরের ভেতরে গড়ে তোলা বিউটি পার্লারে একজন নারীকে সেবা দিচ্ছেন বিউটিশিয়ান তিনি বলেন, ‘আপনার ভেতর শুধুই হতাশা কাজ করে; একেবারে ভেঙে পড়েন। এখন আফগানিস্তানে আনন্দ বা স্বস্তি দেওয়ার মতো আর কিছুই নেই। ভ্রমণ নেই, পার্ক নেই, স্কুল নেই—একেবারে কিছুই নেই। তিনি বলেন, ‘কিন্তু এখন ওরা তা-ও (সেলুন) করতে দেবে না। আফগানিস্তানের নারীদের কাছে কাজ করাটাই যেন অপরাধ হয়ে দাঁড়িয়েছে।’ সেলুন নিষিদ্ধ হলেও তিনি নিজের মতো করে একটি সেলুন খোলার সিদ্ধান্ত নেন। বিশেষ করে বিয়ের অনুষ্ঠানে নারীদের চুলের সাজ ও মেকআপের চাহিদা ছিল বেশ। তিনি একটি ফ্ল্যাট ভাড়া নেন এবং সরঞ্জাম কেনেন। শিগগিরই তাঁর প্রায় ৩০ জন গ্রাহক হয়ে যান। আফগানিস্তানের যে লাখ লাখ পুরুষ কাজ পাচ্ছেন না, তাঁর স্বামীও তাঁদের একজন; তাই এই কাজটিই ছিল তাঁদের বেঁচে থাকার অবলম্বন। কিন্তু তালেবান কর্তৃপক্ষ তাঁর গোপন সেলুনের খোঁজ পেয়ে যায়। অভিযানে সব সরঞ্জাম এবং প্রায় সব আসবাবপত্র নিয়ে যায় তারা। বিয়ের সাজ নিতে আসা নারীতে সেলুন ভরা। বিউটিশিয়ানরা তাঁদের গালে পাউডার বুলিয়ে দিচ্ছেন, আর তাঁরা মেঝেতে গদির ওপর শুয়ে আছেন। পরিবেশটি হালকা মনে হলেও এর নিচে চাপা ভয় কাজ করছিল। সেলুনের মালিক বলেন, ‘দরজায় প্রতিবার কড়া নাড়লেই ভয় হয়, ওপাশে তালেবান দাঁড়িয়ে নেই তো?’ তিনি বলেন, ‘আমি একেবারে দিশেহারা হয়ে পড়েছিলাম। যে কাজটি আমাকে কিছুটা হলেও উদ্দেশ্য খুঁজে দিত, সেটিই যদি কেড়ে নেওয়া হয়, তবে আমার কী রইল? সন্তানদের কীভাবে খাওয়াব? সংসারের খরচ কীভাবে চালাব? আমি চরম হতাশায় পৌঁছে গিয়েছিলাম এবং ভেবেছিলাম, দেশই ছেড়ে চলে যাব।’ কিন্তু গ্রাহকদের ফোন আসতেই থাকে, আর তাঁকে বিলও মেটাতে হয়। শেষ পর্যন্ত তিনি আবার চেষ্টা করার সিদ্ধান্ত নেন। আরেকটি ফ্ল্যাট ভাড়া নিয়ে নতুন করে শুরু করেন। এখন তাঁর সাতজন কর্মী আছেন—তাঁরা সবাই তরুণী এবং নিজেদের পরিবার চালাচ্ছেন। অক্টোবরের সাম্প্রতিক এক দিনে দেখা যায়, বিয়ের সাজ নিতে আসা নারীতে সেলুন ভরা। বিউটিশিয়ানরা তাঁদের গালে পাউডার বুলিয়ে দিচ্ছেন, আর তাঁরা মেঝেতে গদির ওপর শুয়ে আছেন। পরিবেশটি হালকা মনে হলেও এর নিচে চাপা ভয় কাজ করছিল। সেলুনের মালিক বলেন, ‘দরজায় প্রতিবার কড়া নাড়লেই ভয় হয়, ওপাশে তালেবান দাঁড়িয়ে নেই তো?’ ঘরের ভেতরে গড়ে ওঠা স্কুলে পাঠদান কৈশোরে তাঁর সব স্বপ্ন ছিল ফুটবলকে ঘিরে। মনে হচ্ছিল স্বপ্নগুলো সত্যি হতে চলেছে—তিনি জাতীয় দলে সুযোগ পেয়েছিলেন। কিন্তু দুই বছর পর নারী খেলাধুলার ওপর নিষেধাজ্ঞা সেই স্বপ্ন গুঁড়িয়ে দেয়। মানসিক অবসাদে ডুবে গিয়ে তিনি ছয় মাস ঘর থেকে প্রায় বেরই হননি। তাঁর পরিবার চিন্তিত হয়ে পড়ে, আর তিনি বুঝতে পারেন, এই অবস্থা থেকে বের হওয়ার পথ তাঁকে নিজেকেই খুঁজতে হবে। শেষ পর্যন্ত তিনি আবার খেলা শুরু করেন—মাঠে নয়, ঘরের ছোট্ট পরিসরে। বক্সিংও শুরু করেন তিনি; পুরোনো গাড়ির টায়ার জমিয়ে বানিয়ে নেন প্রাথমিক মানের পাঞ্চিং ব্যাগ। তিনি জানান, নিজের আবেগ সামলাতে এটি তাঁকে সাহায্য করেছে। তাঁর আসল ভালোবাসা এখনো ফুটবল। নিজে ঠিকমতো খেলতে না পেরে নতুন প্রজন্মের কাছে নিজের জ্ঞান ও দক্ষতা পৌঁছে দেওয়ার সিদ্ধান্ত নেন। নিজের বাড়ির ছোট্ট দেয়ালঘেরা উঠানে একদল বাচ্চাকে কোচিং করান তিনি। চোখে জল নিয়ে তিনি বলেন, ‘ওদের মধ্যে আমি সেই একই স্বপ্ন ও আবেগ দেখেছি, যা আমার নিজের শৈশবে ছিল। ওদের প্র্যাকটিস করাতে আমার খুব ভালো লাগে। কখনো কখনো ওদের মধ্যে নিজেকেই দেখতে পাই।’ তালেবান শাসনে যেভাবে ঘুরে দাঁড়াচ্ছেন আফগান নারীরা গোপনে পড়াশোনা করে যাচ্ছে আফগান মেয়েরা, দেখছে ভবিষ্যতের স্বপ্ন বক্সিং আর কোচিংয়ের মধ্য দিয়ে কোনোমতে দিন কেটে যায় তাঁর। কিন্তু ভবিষ্যৎ নিয়ে তাঁর দৃষ্টিভঙ্গি অন্ধকারাচ্ছন্ন। তিনি দেশ ছেড়ে অন্য কোনো দেশে আশ্রয় নিতে চান। তিনি বলেন, ‘আফগানিস্তানে নিজের জন্য কোনো আশা দেখি না। আমাদের জন্য কোনো দরজাই খোলা নেই।’ সন্দেহ এড়াতে শিক্ষার্থীরা একে একে আলাদা সময়ে আসে। দরজা সামান্য ফাঁক করে তাদের ভেতরে ঢোকানো হয়। ভেতরে পড়ানো হয় সাধারণ বিষয়ই—ইতিহাস, বিজ্ঞান, ভূগোল, গণিত, ভাষা ও কোরআন শিক্ষা। কিন্তু এটি কোনো সাধারণ স্কুল নয়। একটি ব্যক্তিগত বাড়ির ভেতরে গড়ে তোলা এই স্কুলে ছেলেদের পাশাপাশি ২০ বছর বয়সী মেয়েরাও পড়ে। কিশোরী মেয়েরাও থাকায় ক্লাসগুলো গোপনে নিতে হয়। এখানকার শিক্ষক—২০ বছর বয়সী এক তরুণী, যাঁকে সাহায্য করেন তাঁর কিশোরী বোন—পেশাগতভাবে প্রশিক্ষিত নন। স্কুল বন্ধ হওয়ার আগে তাঁরা যা শিখেছিলেন, সাধ্যমতো তা-ই অন্যদের পৌঁছে দিচ্ছেন। ওই তরুণী বলেন, ‘আফগানিস্তানের বর্তমান পরিস্থিতি মোটেই ভালো নয়। আমি তীব্র মানসিক অবসাদে ভুগছিলাম, তাই এই ক্লাস চালুর সিদ্ধান্ত নিই।’ গোপন স্কুলে কিশোরীদের পড়াশোনা তিনি জানান, এক বছরেরও বেশি সময় আগে তিনি এটি শুরু করেন—মেয়েদের ‘একটু আশার আলো দেখানো এবং পড়াশোনা চালিয়ে যাওয়ার সুযোগ করে দেওয়ার’ আশায়। এখন তাঁর শিক্ষার্থী প্রায় ৩০ জন। বাড়ির একটি কক্ষকে শ্রেণিকক্ষে রূপ দেওয়া হয়েছে; শিক্ষার্থীরা নিচু প্লাস্টিকের টেবিলে মেঝেতে বসে। দেয়ালজুড়ে উজ্জ্বল রঙের আঁকা ছবি। তালেবানের নিষেধাজ্ঞাগুলোর মধ্যে শিক্ষার ওপর বিধিনিষেধই সবচেয়ে বেশি অপছন্দনীয়। কর্মকর্তারা বারবার বলছেন, তাঁরা একটি সমাধানের চেষ্টা করছেন। গত আগস্টে সরকারের মুখপাত্র জাবিউল্লাহ মুজাহিদ বলেন, ‘শিক্ষার যে অংশে এখনো ঘাটতি রয়েছে, তা সার্বিকভাবে সমাধানের জন্য আমরা চেষ্টা করছি।’ কিন্তু অগ্রগতির কোনো লক্ষণ দেখা যায়নি। কিশোরী সহকারী শিক্ষিকা বলেন, অনেক মেয়েই পিছিয়ে পড়েছে, আর ‘আমরা এমন একটি পরিবেশ তৈরি করতে চেয়েছি, যেখানে মেয়েরা পড়াশোনা করতে পারে এবং নিজেদের লক্ষ্যে পৌঁছানোর চেষ্টা করতে পারে।’ কিন্তু প্রতিটি ক্লাস নেওয়ার সময়ই তাঁদের গ্রেপ্তারের ঝুঁকি থাকে। তিনি বলেন, ‘আমরা তালেবানকে ভীষণ ভয় পাই। আমাদের ভয় হয়, একদিন হয়তো ওরা আসবে, নিয়ম ভাঙার অভিযোগ তুলবে, গ্রেপ্তার করে ধরে নিয়ে যাবে। এই আশঙ্কায় আমরা একেবারে আতঙ্কিত হয়ে থাকি।’ এলেনা বেকাতোরোস দক্ষিণ-পূর্ব ইউরোপে এপির ব্যুরো প্রধান। অ্যাসোসিয়েটেড প্রেসের হয়ে দক্ষিণ-পূর্ব ইউরোপের সংবাদ কভারেজের তত্ত্বাবধান করেন বেকাতোরোস; পাশাপাশি মধ্যপ্রাচ্য ও আফগানিস্তানেও তিনি নিয়মিত অ্যাসাইনমেন্টে যান। গ্রিসের এথেন্সভিত্তিক এই সাংবাদিক বলকান, ইরাক, আফগানিস্তান ও ইউক্রেনের যুদ্ধ কভার করাসহ বিশ্বের নানা প্রান্তে কাজ করেছেন। দ্য ইন্ডিপেন্ডেন্ট থেকে নেওয়া। ইংরেজি থেকে নেওয়া।

articles.title: যুক্তরাষ্ট্রের শুল্কনীতি বাংলাদেশের অর্থনীতির জন্য কী ঝুঁকি তৈরি করছে
articles.fullText: যুক্তরাষ্ট্র বাংলাদেশের পণ্য রপ্তানির ওপর সর্বোচ্চ ১৮ শতাংশ অতিরিক্ত শুল্ক আরোপের প্রস্তাব করেছে। ১৯৭৪ সালের মার্কিন বাণিজ্য আইনের ৩০১ ধারার আওতায় এই উদ্যোগের পক্ষে ওয়াশিংটনের যুক্তি হলো, বাংলাদেশের শিল্পনীতি, রপ্তানি প্রণোদনা, উৎপাদন সক্ষমতা ও শ্রমমান আন্তর্জাতিক প্রতিযোগিতাকে প্রভাবিত করছে এবং মার্কিন উৎপাদকদের অসুবিধায় ফেলছে। তবে এ ধরনের পদক্ষেপের যৌক্তিকতা নিয়ে প্রশ্ন রয়েছে। বাংলাদেশের শিল্প সম্প্রসারণ ও রপ্তানি প্রবৃদ্ধি মূলত দেশের উন্নয়নের কৌশল, তুলনামূলক সুবিধা এবং বৈশ্বিক সরবরাহব্যবস্থায় অংশগ্রহণের ফল। রপ্তানি প্রণোদনা কিংবা উৎপাদনের সক্ষমতা বৃদ্ধি করলেই তা অন্যায্য বাণিজ্যচর্চার প্রমাণ হয়ে যায় না। একটি উন্নয়নশীল দেশের পণ্যের ওপর উচ্চ শুল্ক আরোপ করে একটি শিল্পোন্নত দেশের অভ্যন্তরীণ শিল্পকে সুরক্ষা দেওয়ার উদ্যোগ আন্তর্জাতিক বাণিজ্যে ন্যায্যতা এবং নিয়মভিত্তিক বহুপক্ষীয় বাণিজ্যব্যবস্থার নীতির সঙ্গেও সাংঘর্ষিক কি না, সে প্রশ্ন তৈরি করে। শুল্ক নিয়ে ট্রাম্পের ছিনিমিনি রুখতে এখনই যা জরুরি যুক্তরাষ্ট্রের পাল্টা শুল্ক: সামনের চ্যালেঞ্জ মোকাবিলায় আরও যা ভাবা দরকার যুক্তরাষ্ট্রের এই উদ্যোগ বিশ্ববাণিজ্যে একতরফা এবং নীতিবিরোধী পদক্ষেপের প্রবণতাকে আরও স্পষ্ট করেছে। এর ফলে বৈশ্বিক বাণিজ্যব্যবস্থা ক্রমেই অনিশ্চিত হয়ে উঠছে। শুল্কনীতির ঘন ঘন পরিবর্তন রপ্তানিকারক, বিনিয়োগকারী এবং আন্তর্জাতিক বাজারের ওপর নির্ভরশীল ব্যবসাপ্রতিষ্ঠানগুলোর মধ্যে অনিশ্চয়তা সৃষ্টি করে। বাংলাদেশের মতো উন্নয়নশীল দেশের জন্য এ ধরনের অনিশ্চয়তা বিশেষভাবে ব্যয়বহুল; কারণ, আকস্মিক বাণিজ্যনীতির পরিবর্তন মোকাবিলার সক্ষমতা তাদের তুলনামূলকভাবে সীমিত। প্রস্তাবিত শুল্ক বাংলাদেশের রপ্তানি প্রতিযোগিতায় প্রভাব ফেলতে পারে। যুক্তরাষ্ট্র বাংলাদেশের একক বৃহত্তম রপ্তানি গন্তব্য। মার্কিন বাণিজ্য পরিসংখ্যান অনুযায়ী, ২০২৫ সালে বাংলাদেশ যুক্তরাষ্ট্রে প্রায় ৯ দশমিক ৪৭ বিলিয়ন ডলারের পণ্য রপ্তানি করেছে, যা ২০২৪ সালের ৮ দশমিক ৩৬ বিলিয়ন ডলারের চেয়ে বেশি। ২০২৫ সালে এই রপ্তানির মধ্যে তৈরি পোশাকের পরিমাণ ছিল প্রায় ৮ দশমিক ২ বিলিয়ন ডলার। একতরফা বাণিজ্যনীতির প্রভাবে পরিবর্তনশীল বৈশ্বিক পরিবেশে বাংলাদেশকে নিজের ন্যায্য বাণিজ্যিক স্বার্থ রক্ষার পাশাপাশি অর্থনীতির অভ্যন্তরীণ সক্ষমতাও বাড়াতে হবে। কার্যকর কূটনৈতিক উদ্যোগ, প্রয়োজনীয় সংস্কার ও রপ্তানি বহুমুখীকরণই হতে পারে টেকসই রপ্তানি প্রবৃদ্ধি নিশ্চিত করার প্রধান ভিত্তি। এ পরিসংখ্যান দুই দেশের বাণিজ্যে পোশাক খাতের গুরুত্ব স্পষ্ট করে। উচ্চ শুল্কের ফলে মার্কিন আমদানিকারকদের জন্য বাংলাদেশি পণ্যের ব্যয় বাড়তে পারে এবং তাঁরা বিকল্প দেশ থেকে পণ্য সংগ্রহে উৎসাহিত হতে পারেন। অন্যদিকে মার্কিন ক্রেতারা অতিরিক্ত শুল্কের চাপ সামলাতে বাংলাদেশি রপ্তানিকারকদের কাছ থেকে পণ্যের দাম কমানোর দাবি জানাতে পারেন। এতে রপ্তানিকারকদের মুনাফা ও বিনিয়োগের সক্ষমতা কমে যাওয়ার আশঙ্কা রয়েছে। এর প্রভাব শুধু রপ্তানি আয়ের মধ্যে সীমাবদ্ধ থাকবে না। তৈরি পোশাকশিল্পে লাখ লাখ মানুষের কর্মসংস্থান রয়েছে। এ খাতের সঙ্গে পরিবহন, প্যাকেজিং, সরবরাহ, ব্যাংকিংসহ বহু সহযোগী শিল্প ও সেবা খাত জড়িত। রপ্তানি আদেশ কমে গেলে উৎপাদন, কর্মসংস্থান ও পারিবারিক আয় ক্ষতিগ্রস্ত হতে পারে। একই সঙ্গে বৈদেশিক মুদ্রা অর্জনের ওপরও চাপ সৃষ্টি হতে পারে। তাই বিষয়টি শুধু পোশাক রপ্তানিকারকদের সমস্যা হিসেবে দেখার সুযোগ নেই; এটি সামগ্রিক অর্থনৈতিক ব্যবস্থাপনার সঙ্গেও সম্পর্কিত। ট্রাম্পের শুল্ক আরোপ, বাংলাদেশের সামনে পথ কী ট্রাম্পের প্রতিশোধমূলক শুল্ক থেকে বাংলাদেশ যেভাবে লাভবান হতে পারে এ পরিস্থিতি বাংলাদেশের সীমিতসংখ্যক পণ্য ও বাজারের ওপর অতিরিক্ত নির্ভরতার দুর্বলতাও সামনে এনেছে। তৈরি পোশাক খাত অর্থনৈতিক প্রবৃদ্ধিতে গুরুত্বপূর্ণ অবদান রাখলেও এ নির্ভরতা আন্তর্জাতিক বাণিজ্যনীতির পরিবর্তনের মুখে অর্থনীতিকে ঝুঁকিপূর্ণ করে তোলে। এ ঝুঁকি কমাতে ওষুধ, চামড়াজাত পণ্য, জুতা, কৃষি প্রক্রিয়াজাত পণ্য, হালকা প্রকৌশল এবং তথ্যপ্রযুক্তি খাতে রপ্তানি বহুমুখীকরণ জরুরি। এ পরিস্থিতিতে তিনটি পদক্ষেপকে অগ্রাধিকার দেওয়া প্রয়োজন। প্রথমত, যুক্তরাষ্ট্রের সঙ্গে তথ্য-প্রমাণভিত্তিক আলোচনার মাধ্যমে প্রস্তাবিত শুল্কের যৌক্তিকতা চ্যালেঞ্জ করতে হবে এবং বাংলাদেশের জন্য অনুকূল সিদ্ধান্ত আদায়ের চেষ্টা চালাতে হবে। দ্বিতীয়ত, যুক্তরাষ্ট্র ও তৈরি পোশাক খাতের ওপর নির্ভরতা কমাতে রপ্তানি পণ্য ও বাজারের বহুমুখীকরণ ত্বরান্বিত করতে হবে। তৃতীয়ত, রপ্তানি প্রতিযোগিতা সক্ষমতা বাড়াতে শিল্পের উৎপাদনশীলতা, প্রযুক্তিগত আধুনিকায়ন, অবকাঠামো ও শ্রমমান উন্নয়নে বিনিয়োগ বাড়াতে হবে। সর্বোপরি একতরফা বাণিজ্যনীতির প্রভাবে পরিবর্তনশীল বৈশ্বিক পরিবেশে বাংলাদেশকে নিজের ন্যায্য বাণিজ্যিক স্বার্থ রক্ষার পাশাপাশি অর্থনীতির অভ্যন্তরীণ সক্ষমতাও বাড়াতে হবে। কার্যকর কূটনৈতিক উদ্যোগ, প্রয়োজনীয় সংস্কার ও রপ্তানি বহুমুখীকরণই হতে পারে টেকসই রপ্তানি প্রবৃদ্ধি নিশ্চিত করার প্রধান ভিত্তি। সেলিম রায়হান অর্থনীতির অধ্যাপক, ঢাকা বিশ্ববিদ্যালয় এবং নির্বাহী পরিচালক, সানেম

Women and girls are not getting any safer
articles.excerpt: Legal protections and societal support needed for women's safety
articles.fullText:
Child marriage is also on the rise, increasing the risk of sexual and other forms of violence against children. ASK has found reports of at least 87 victims of dowry-related violence, with 48 women and girls killed after physical torture. A report in this daily shows how even after divorce, around 52 percent faced physical and emotional abuse.

These statistics highlight the failure of the state and society to keep women and girls safe. Despite having stringent laws to prosecute perpetrators of such violence, enforcement is weak and conviction rates are very low. The legal system is fraught with loopholes and inefficiencies that ultimately victimise the survivors further and embolden the perpetrators. The Child Marriage Restraint Act, 2017, for instance, has allowed parents and guardians to marry off underage girls.

The law that deals with violence against women and children, which was enacted two decades ago, established specialised tribunals to deliver swift trials and severe punishments within 180 days. But the ground realities of overburdened tribunals, with a severe shortage of judges and staff, have resulted in less than 3 percent of convictions. Cases become weak due to long delays with evidence being lost, witnesses becoming unavailable and victims or their families often being intimidated to withdraw cases.

The government’s first step, therefore, has to be developing a legal system that protects women and girls inside their homes and outside. Helplines must be accessible, tribunals must be adequately equipped, there must be enough safe houses for victims and adequate state legal support. Specialised gender-based training is needed in the courts and police stations. The police’s investigative capacity needs to be strengthened. Witness protection, confidential reporting and counselling survivors of violence must be prioritised.

Additionally, public spaces, offices and educational institutions must have safeguards to prevent violence against women and girls. How society perceives women significantly influences the level of violence they face. Here too, the government must play a role in ensuring that women are treated as equal citizens and valued for their significant contributions towards the development and prosperity of the nation.

articles.title: When justice keeps getting another deadline
articles.excerpt: The problem extends far beyond Bangladesh. Unesco reports that at least 1,641 journalists and media workers were killed worldwide between 2006 and 2025.
articles.fullText:
Recent developments have exposed troubling gaps in coordination. In August 2026, the chief prosecutor of the International Crimes Tribunal (ICT) said preliminary evidence suggested a possible link to a cultural figure, while a PBI official noted that the investigation team had not received that information. In September, the ICT chief prosecutor said the prosecution would examine whether the tribunal had jurisdiction after receiving an application from the victims’ family. Meanwhile, PBI said it had requested digital evidence and data preserved by the tribunal but had not received the material. The ICT prosecution, on the other hand, said it would share its findings with PBI after further investigation and verification.

A 27-page progress report submitted to the High Court reveals how much remains unresolved. Previous investigators recorded statements from 167 witnesses; the current investigation officer questioned 90 and formally recorded statements from 24. Scientific examinations indicated that both journalists had been murdered, with no evidence supporting the theory that one spouse killed the other and then died by suicide over marital or family disputes.

The two laptops and mobile phone reportedly taken from the flat have not been recovered. The investigation has generated activity, reports, and repeated deadlines. What it has not delivered is an account of who killed Sagar and Runi and why. For the families, the delays are not merely procedural. In an interview with The Daily Star , Sagar’s 74-year-old mother said she hoped to see those responsible brought to justice in her lifetime. She also said no one from the current task force had contacted her of late.

Crucially, the stakes extend beyond one family. In June 2026, the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) urged Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to honour his commitment to press freedom, noting that it had documented at least 10 incidents of violence and harassment against reporters covering political events in 2025. This was a category-specific count, and the situation remained concerning in 2026 as well.

The Human Rights Support Society (HRSS) recorded 86 incidents of violations of freedom of expression affecting 111 people between January and October, including 25 journalists. Meanwhile, following criticism of its September proposals, the government published a revised draft of the cyber-law amendments on November 10. The proposed maximum prison sentence for spreading rumours or disinformation was reduced from 10 to five years, but these remained criminal offences, with concerns persisting over the scope of enforcement powers and safeguards for independent journalism.

The problem extends far beyond Bangladesh. Unesco reports that at least 1,641 journalists and media workers were killed worldwide between 2006 and 2025 . In 2024 and 2025 alone, 189 journalists and media workers were killed, while the global impunity rate for journalist killings rose to 86 percent.

It’s important to note that transparency does not require disclosing every investigative lead, exposing sensitive evidence, or compromising witnesses. It requires credible updates, within legal limits, on a case’s status and the reasons for delay. Extensions may sometimes be justified, but repeated extensions demand scrutiny. On October 27, 2026 , the High Court directed the task force to complete its investigation and submit a report by April 29, 2027. It also ordered the task force head and an ICT prosecutor to appear with relevant documents. The order creates an opportunity for scrutiny, but an order is not an outcome.

Bangladesh should call for clearer explanations whenever investigation deadlines are extended, including what work remains and what steps are expected next. Investigative and prosecutorial bodies should clarify their responsibilities and ensure relevant leads and evidence are lawfully assessed and shared. After all, impunity persists not only when perpetrators escape punishment, but also when investigations fail to establish the truth and accountability is postponed indefinitely.

Ashfaq Ferdous is lecturer of sociology at Southeast University and former assistant superintendent of police with Bangladesh Police.

COP31 failed, but a weak climate deal would have been worse
articles.excerpt: The UN climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye ended on November 22 without an agreed outcome. After running roughly two days past its scheduled end, the Turkish COP presidency declared there would be no further text.
articles.fullText:
COP31 failed because several structural weaknesses converged: a consensus rule that rewards blockers, a deal text that tried to paper over two contradictory demands, a finance track corroded by distrust, and a presidency structure that lacked the leverage to force a bargain. Conversely, it argues that the collapse, uncomfortable as it is, may be less damaging than the weak deal that would have pushed further retreats.

The conference’s draft text named no fossil fuels, while focusing language prominently on carbon capture. On adaptation finance, it removed the target of $120 billion a year and substituted talks on a pathway to triple adaptation finance by 2035, with no agreed baseline to triple from. The opposing camp was formidable—Saudi Arabia, Russia, and the Arab Group, with India and China sharing red lines inside a broader developing-country bloc. Against them stood more than 130 countries that had reportedly called for a roadmap away from fossil fuels. This was a stark retreat from COP28 and COP30 on the transition away from fossil fuels and tripling of adaptation finance. The majority could not prevail because the process does not count heads.

The consensus rule for decision-making turns minorities into veto holders, with no practicable voting procedure to break a deadlock. In practice, “consensus” has come to mean the absence of any formal objection, so a single powerful party can hold a text hostage. At COP30, roughly 80 countries backed a fossil fuel roadmap, but it was pushed out of a formal decision into a voluntary presidency process . The critical point is that consensus is not inherently the problem; it is the interaction between consensus and an issue where some members’ economic growth is at stake. Then the draft cover decision, as a political package, asked to do the impossible: accelerate renewables, raise finance, and acknowledge that the 1.5 degrees Celsius limit is soon to be breached.

Packaging everything into one cover decision means the most contested paragraph can sink the whole. The presidency’s strategy of omitting fossil fuels to secure its opponents bought nothing, because it cost the support of the EU and vulnerable states. A draft built around lowest-common-denominator language can lose both flanks at once, and here it did so.

A further irony is that the omission was not even the compromise it appeared to be. COP28 in Dubai had already agreed to transition away from fossil fuels. Dropping the phrase therefore looked less like neutrality than outright retreat from an agreed position, which is why the EU and small island states framed it as unacceptable. Then, finance had more to do with a trust deficit. The adaptation finance dispute illustrates how vague promises compound distrust. Developing countries have watched earlier pledges, including the $300 billion Baku goal , with little funding ring-fenced for adaptation and with a heavy reliance on loans rather than grants. When rich countries are themselves under budget pressure from wars, energy costs, and domestic politics, they are reluctant to commit to precise figures. Vulnerable countries, in turn, read vagueness as bad faith. The result is a stalemate, where neither side trusts the other enough to move.

Furthermore, the unusual arrangement of a dual COP presidency created a division of labour, but also blurred accountability. Australia itself is a major fossil fuel exporter, which critics say limited its credibility as an honest broker on the central issue. Civil society groups accused the presidency of caving to carbon capture interests, and one analysis counted hundreds of carbon capture lobbyists accredited to the conference. Lobbying numbers on their own prove little causation, but they feed a perception of a process captured, which weakens the moral authority needed to broker a hard bargain. Conversely , some observers suggest that failure may be preferable to a text that cannot even name the central problem. There is force in this argument. If the EU had accepted the draft, a COP outcome omitting fossil fuels would have become the second in a row, normalising the omission. Rejecting it preserves the Dubai language as the reference point and signals that silence is no longer a price worth paying for unanimity.

But the argument has limits. A collapse also forfeits whatever modest gains the package contained, including the adaptation finance pathway that vulnerable countries need. Reporting indicates that agriculture negotiations also broke down, so the costs are not confined to the headline text. The collapse is therefore best described as a refusal to ratify a retreat, not as a success. Importantly, it does not erase earlier commitments, and the Paris Agreement and previous COP decisions remain in force.

In the end, Antalya failed for reasons that were visible all along. A consensus system that empowers minorities, a package that tried to satisfy opposing red lines with ambiguity, a finance relationship built on unverifiable promises, and a presidency without the leverage to compel agreement made a breakdown close to predictable. So the collapse is best read as a stress test that the process failed, but also as a refusal to normalise silence about fossil fuels, which is the cardinal problem of climate change.

Dr Mizan R Khan is a climate negotiator since 2001 and technical lead at LDC Universities Consortium on Climate Change (LUCCC).
